tip_title: Your Kids Are Almost Out of the House. Does Your Life Insurance Number Still Make Sense?
topic: life insurance coverage adequacy - empty nester and college-cost recalculation angle
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Kids Are Almost Out of the House. Does Your Life Insurance Number Still Make Sense?**

Most people set their life insurance coverage amount once — usually when the kids were young and the mortgage was new — and never revisit it. But the number that made sense ten years ago might not match where you actually are today. If your kids are heading to college or already out of the house, your income-replacement needs shift. So does the debt picture. The standard framework is to add up what you'd want to cover: remaining mortgage, outstanding debts, income your household would need to replace, and any education costs still on the horizon. Then compare that to what your current policy actually pays out. A lot of people are surprised by the gap in both directions — either way too much or not nearly enough.

Not sure if your current coverage still fits? Your Peachy agent can help you run the numbers and see where you stand.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/how-much-life-insurance-do-i-need)
summary: Covers life insurance coverage adequacy as a recalculation exercise for households in the empty-nester or near-empty-nester life stage, framed as a periodic review of whether the original coverage amount still matches current debt, income-replacement, and education-cost needs.
scoring_notes: Prior life insurance coverage tip (June 22) was framed as a general income-replacement and debt-addition framework for evaluating an existing policy. This tip targets a specific life-stage trigger: kids heading to or already in college, which is highly relevant for both audiences right now (August, back-to-school season, established families and empty nesters). The angle is the life-stage recalculation prompt rather than the general how-to-check framing. Strong fit for East Cobb (median age 42, family skew with teens and college-age kids). Diversifies away from home category. Source is iii.org, top-tier trusted source.

tip_title: Your Roof Is the First Thing Your Insurer Looks At After a Storm. Is It in Good Shape?
topic: water damage home insurance coverage - roof and structural maintenance angle
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Roof Is the First Thing Your Insurer Looks At After a Storm. Is It in Good Shape?**

Here's something a lot of homeowners find out the hard way: if your roof was already worn down or poorly maintained before a storm rolled through, your homeowners policy may not cover the water damage that follows. Coverage applies when damage is sudden and accidental — not when it develops because a structure wasn't kept up. That matters a lot right now, with late summer storm season still in full swing. A roof in rough shape isn't just a home maintenance issue; it's a coverage issue. Before a storm gives you a reason to file a claim, it's worth doing a quick visual check and knowing where your roof stands.

Not sure how condition or age affects what your policy covers? Your Peachy agent can walk through what your policy actually says — it's a quicker conversation than you'd think.

📖 [Learn more from Policygenius](https://www.policygenius.com/homeowners-insurance/does-homeowners-insurance-cover-water-damage-from-rain/)
summary: Covers the homeowners insurance rule that water damage from rain is not covered when poor structural maintenance (specifically roof condition) is a contributing factor, framed as a late-summer storm-season action item to inspect before filing a claim.
scoring_notes: Repeat subject area (water damage) but distinct angle: prior tip (June 29) covered the sudden-vs-gradual exclusion mechanic in general terms; this tip is specifically about roof and structural maintenance as the trigger for a denial, framed as a pre-storm inspection action item during peak late-summer storm season. High timeliness — August 29, still deep in storm season. Strong fit for both audiences: 78% homeownership in East Cobb, high homeownership in both. Source is policygenius.com, on trusted list.
